title: Correlated defaults
objectives: See how a shared cause makes defaults cluster in a loan portfolio
Find a portfolio's tail risk by total probability over regimes
Explain why diversification fails against a common factor

screens.title: Correlated defaults
screens.prose: A bank lends to ten borrowers, and each one rarely defaults. What matters is whether bad years hit them one at a time or all at once.

state.caption: Ten borrowers, each defaulting with chance 0.05, independently

options.text: It rises

options.why: You kept the average fixed and expected the risk to stay fixed. A shared shock bunches the defaults into the same years.

options.text: It falls: most years are now calmer
options.why: Most years are calmer. But the bad years now bring several defaults at once.

explain.text: A recession pushes all ten chances up in the same year, so defaults come in clusters. Calm years get calmer and bad years get worse. Each borrower still defaults 5% of the time, but the tail grows.

explain.text: Add the two paths: $0.2 \times 0.2^2 + 0.8 \times 0.0125^2 = 0.008125$. Independence would give $0.05^2 = 0.0025$. Two defaults together are more than three times as likely.

screens.prose: Now the whole book of ten. Inside each regime the defaults are independent trials, so the binomial gives each regime's tail. The leaves show $P(3 \text{ or more defaults})$ in each regime.

byKey.indep: That is the independent answer. Here the defaults share the economy.

explain.text: Total probability over the regimes gives $0.2 \times 0.3222 + 0.8 \times 0.0002 = 0.0646$. That is 5.6 times the 0.0115 for independent defaults. Almost all of it comes from the recession branch.

screens.prose: A risk model knows each borrower defaults with chance 0.05. It also knows that, given the economy, defaults are independent. So it reports $P(3 \text{ or more}) = 0.0115$ from a binomial with $p = 0.05$.

screens.prose: You split the book by regime, used independent trials inside each, then added. With $K$ the number of defaults, $$P(K \ge 3) = \sum_{\text{regimes } r} P(r)\,P(K \ge 3 \mid r).$$ Inside each regime, $P(K \ge 3 \mid r)$ is a binomial tail.
screens.question: Which assumption lets you use the binomial inside each regime?

options.text: Defaults are independent given the regime
Defaults are independent overall
options.why: They are not: you saw them cluster. Independence holds only once the regime is fixed.

options.text: Every borrower has chance 0.05
options.why: In a recession the chance is 0.2, not 0.05. Each regime's binomial uses its own chance.

hints.text: What did you assume when you multiplied along the two-borrower paths?
Inside a regime you multiplied the borrowers' chances. That needs independence given the regime.

feedback.correct: Independence given the regime; total probability does the rest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what you multiplied inside each regime.

explain.text: Inside a regime you multiplied the borrowers' chances: independence given the regime. Total probability then weights each regime. That pair of steps is the whole method.

screens.title: The book in code
screens.prose: A recession comes with chance `q`. Then each loan defaults with chance `p_bad`, and otherwise `p_good`. Given the regime, loans default independently. `tail` is the binomial tail from Independent trials.
screens.question: Complete `book_tail` so it returns the chance of `k` or more defaults among `n` loans.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Each answer is accepted when it is within a relative error of 1e-9 of the exact value.

hints.text: Split by regime, as on the tree.
Use `tail(k, n, p_bad)` for the recession branch and `tail(k, n, p_good)` for the other.
`return q * tail(k, n, p_bad) + (1 - q) * tail(k, n, p_good)`

feedback.correct: Total probability over the two regimes, binomial inside each.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Weight each regime's tail by its chance and add.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that the `...` is replaced.

explain.text:
Each regime contributes its chance times its own binomial tail. For our book, `book_tail(3, 10, 0.2, 0.2, 0.0125)` gives 0.0646. The example checks the two-borrower answer, 0.008125.

```python
return q * tail(k, n, p_bad) + (1 - q) * tail(k, n, p_good)
```

screens.prose: A bank pools the ten loans and sells two slices. The junior slice absorbs the first 2 defaults. The senior slice loses only if 3 or more default. Before 2008, many models priced such slices as if mortgage defaults were independent.

state.caption: Bars: shared economy. Dashed: independent defaults. The senior slice is hit in the last bar.

screens.question: Why was the senior slice riskier than those models said?

options.text: A shared factor, falling house prices, made defaults cluster: 3 or more became far likelier
Each loan was riskier than its stated chance
options.why: That can happen too, but here each loan's 0.05 is right. The models failed on how defaults combine.

options.text: Ten loans are too few; a thousand would have been safe
options.why: More loans do not remove a shared factor. In a recession every loan's chance rises together, however many there are.

options.text: The junior slice was too thin to protect anyone
options.why: The junior slice did its job for scattered defaults. Clustered defaults went straight through it.

hints.text: Compare the last bar with its dashed line.
The senior slice loses only in this bar.
With a shared factor the senior slice is hit with chance 0.0646, not 0.0115.

feedback.correct: A common factor turns rare joint losses into a real risk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what made several mortgages default in the same year.

explain.text: With a shared factor, the senior slice is hit with chance 0.0646, not 0.0115: 5.6 times the modelled risk. Diversifying across loans removes separate risks, not shared ones. In 2008 falling house prices were the shared factor.

ideas: A shared factor makes defaults independent given the regime but correlated overall, though each borrower's own chance is unchanged.
Find the book's tail by total probability: weight each regime's binomial tail by the regime's chance and add. Here $0.0646$, not $0.0115$.
Diversification removes separate risks, not shared ones. Senior slices fail when defaults cluster.

quiz.prose: Use the lesson's model: recession chance 0.2, default chance 0.2 in a recession and 0.0125 otherwise. Imagine a pool of very many such loans.

options.why: Averaging removes separate risks. In a recession about 20% of a large pool defaults, every time.

options.text: About 0.05, the default chance
options.why: 0.05 is one loan's chance. The pool's bad years come with the recession.

options.text: Close to 1

feedback.correct: A large pool defaults at its regime's rate: 20% in a recession, 1.25% otherwise.

explain.text: In a large pool the share that defaults is close to the regime's chance: 20% in a recession, 1.25% otherwise. So at least 10% default exactly in recession years, chance 0.2. Size diversifies away separate risk, never the shared factor.
